summary: Tipaza, the capital of Algeria’s Tipaza Province, is a coastal town founded in 1857 whose ancient predecessor, Tipasa, developed from a Punic trading-post into a Roman military colony and Christian center. Its ancient ruins support tourism, its surroundings are home to the Chenoua people, and its nearby longwave transmitter carries French language Channel 3 programs on 252 kHz.

coreControversy.regulatoryOrHistoricalPrecedent: An ancient Punic trading-post conquered by Rome became a military colony under Claudius for the conquest of the kingdoms of Mauretania, then a municipium called Colonia Aelia Tipasensis.

hiddenCatchesAndLimits: The modern town founded in 1857 is distinct chronologically from ancient Tipasa, which experienced destruction in 430 CE, Byzantine reconstruction one century later, and demolition at the end of the seventh century.
The transmitter’s reported resumption at 252 kHz followed an interruption beginning March 17, 2014; its service was not continuous across that period.
The 20,000 inhabitants figure concerns the fourth century and is attributed to Stéphane Gsell; nearly 30,000 inhabitants describes the modern town in the narrative.

fitAdvice: Tipaza’s ancient ruins are a principal reason for its importance as a tourist destination in modern Algeria; the town is also noted for its sandy littoral.
The town and its surroundings are home to the Chenoua people, described as western Algeria’s largest Berber-speaking group, and the majority of the Bouriba family reside in the area.
